rows.description: I was scolded for something my friend also did. I feel it is unfair and I go quiet and cross. A wise adult listens to my side. The immature pattern is sulking, being rude to the teacher or blaming a friend to escape.

A teacher laughs at my mistake or calls me lazy or silly in front of everyone. I feel small and afraid of school. This is not my fault; telling a parent helps. Children need correction without ridicule.

The teacher shows me gently how to hold the pencil again and smiles. I feel helped, not judged. I learn that being corrected is part of learning and does not mean I am bad, and I try again with pride.

The teacher says my name sternly in front of the class. My face burns and I want to hide. Wise help is a quiet talk after and a chance to fix it. A harsh public telling-off can make a child feel bad instead of learning what to do.
I want to hit back so he stops. Anger is understandable, but fighting can get me punished and hurt. Wise: walk away, stay near friends, report it. Plotting revenge keeps me tied to him.
Bullying makes me feel nobody wants me. That belief is what the bully creates, not the truth. I reach for one safe friend or a club where I fit. Isolation grows in secrecy, so I say it aloud.

Classmates laugh at a photo of me in the class group chat. It hurts and feels public. Wise: do not reply in anger, save the screenshot, tell a parent or teacher. It is not my fault and it can be stopped.

I dread the bus and my stomach hurts on school mornings. Fear is a sensible signal, not weakness. Wise: tell a trusted adult and note what happens. Hiding it because of shame keeps the bully in charge.
My friend tells me a secret and I feel special and responsible. Keeping it shows I am trustworthy. A wise friend keeps it unless someone could be hurt, then tells a trusted adult and explains why.
I told a friend something private and she kept it and just listened. I feel lighter and closer to her. Good friends prove themselves in small quiet ways, and I can repay that trust.
I keep asking a friend what she is hiding. Curiosity is human, but pressing invades her space. Wise: say I am here if you want to talk and then let it go. Trust means giving her the choice.
The secret is so juicy and I want to tell one other person. I remind myself trust is fragile and a betrayal cannot be undone. If I keep it, I grow trustworthy. If I slip, I own up and apologise.

I copied a result to meet a deadline and cannot sleep. Guilt is a signal. Wise: correct it, admit it early to the right person, and learn from the pressure that led there. Harmful: burying it and hoping nobody checks.

A friendly colleague asks me to keep quiet about his shortcut. Loyalty and honesty collide. Wise: urge him to fix it first, and be clear that I cannot lie for him. Harmful: joining the silence until it becomes my problem.
A client hints at a gift if I speed up his file "quietly". I feel flattered and unsafe. Wise: refuse clearly, report per policy, and treat small favours as the start of a larger hold on me.

My boss tells me to backdate a document "just this once" because everyone does. My heart races. Wise: say I am not comfortable, offer a proper alternative, and keep a record. Harmful: complying and calling it obedience.
A friend says everyone messes up and stays with me. I feel a weight lift. Wise: let their view soften mine, and offer the same to others.
I acknowledge the mistake, feel the sting, and treat myself kindly enough to fix it. Wise: kindness and high standards work together.
A mentor tells me they made worse mistakes at my age. I feel hope. Wise: seek people who share their honest stories.
My parent is upset with me after a serious mistake. I feel worthless. Wise: separate my act from my self; apologise, repair, and ask for a chance to earn trust.

I discover my partner took credit, funds, or a deal behind my back and feel shock and rage. I secure records, seek legal and trusted advice, and confront calmly; public smearing or revenge usually harms me too.

My partner keeps making me carry more work for less credit or pay and I feel used but afraid to lose the venture. I state the imbalance, propose a written fix, and prepare to walk away if nothing changes.
My co-founder gets the media credit and investor attention and I feel invisible and bitter. I say it to them directly, agree on fair credit and roles, and avoid quietly undermining them.
I cut a corner or hid a decision from my co-founder and now feel uneasy. I come clean early, offer repair, and restore agreements; excuses like it was for the company's good will not rebuild trust.
